gotchas: No vtable, so no +4 shift: WTargetable's ~WTargetable is non-virtual (RemoveReference calls it directly; PS2's delete-flag argument is just the GCC 2.95 dtor ABI, not a sign of a vtable). Fields 0x0-0x3c line up exactly between the builds. A script that applies +4 to every class that has a namespace of methods would be wrong for all four classes.

bool is 4 bytes on PS2 (GCC 2.95 EE: every bool is sw/lw) and 1 byte on Xbox. A single bool followed by padding stays put (+0x0c, +0x18, +0x38), but two adjacent bools get packed on Xbox: PS2 +0x40/+0x44 become Xbox +0x40/+0x41, and the PS2 +0x48 owner moves to Xbox +0x44. That is -3 and -4, not +4. Read the width from Xbox MOV byte vs dword, then re-pack; never copy PS2 offsets past the first bool pair.

The class size can't be computed from the fields. Both builds use FastAlloc/FastFree(0x50), but the last Xbox field ends at 0x48 (PS2 at 0x4c). Take the size from the alloc and free constants and leave the tail undefined. Don't invent a field there.

The decompiler drops thiscall ECX adjustments. In the ctors, `WSimpleZone::SetPosition(this)` is really ECX=this+0x1c (LEA ECX,[ESI+0x1c]) with `this` as the argument, so there is an embedded WSimpleZone at +0x1c. In InitEffects, `CARP::BaseDesc::CalcDamageZone(effect)` hides ECX=this->baseDesc. Calls like WTargetable::UpdatePosition()/DistFromScreenPos(pt) show no object at all. Take the receiver, and so the member type and offset, from the disassembly.

Ghidra prints offsets in element units of whatever type it guessed. In the Xbox ctor, `param_1_00[0xf]=1` is +0x3c, `*(undefined1*)(param_1_00+0x10)=1` is +0x40 and `*(undefined1*)(param_1_00+3)` is +0x0c. In the resolvers, CARP::TagReference is a 1-byte placeholder, so `this+0x34` really is +0x34 and `this+0x10` steps 16 bytes. But `pCVar5 + puVar2[2]` over CARP__Instance* scales by 64. Parse the disassembly, or scale by the pointee size.

The PS2 vector idioms corrupt widths. Vec3 copies are ldl/ldr 8-byte pairs plus a word. VU0 code loads 128 bits with lqc2 from a 12-byte position, which pulls the next field in as w: WTargetable +0x0c 'visible' shows up as field3 of the position in PS2 DistFromCamera. Width inference on PS2 would merge position+visible into one COORD4. Take widths from Xbox only.

CARP records are file data, identical on both builds. They have no vptr, no Vec3 padding difference and no byte swap (both little-endian). So neither the +4 rule nor the 'PS2 pads COORD3 to 16' rule applies. The PS2 offsets carry over 1:1 (checked for Instance +0x30/+0x3c, BaseDesc +0x10..+0x28/+0x3c/+0x40..+0x58/+0x60, MapNode +0x0/+0x4/+0x8/+0xa/+0xc..+0xf).

CARP::Instance looks like a MATRIX4 but isn't one. Every reader copies 16 dwords and then overwrites the w column (0,0,0,1), because the w slots hold non-float data: a flags byte, a byte and a ushort at +0x0c/+0x0d/+0x0e, a pointer at +0x1c and a packed bitfield at +0x3c. The existing Ghidra type (transform MATRIX4) makes the decompiler print `(uint)transform.mtx[3][3] & 0x3ff` and `mtx[1][3]` used as a pointer. A script that types by 'copied as 16 floats' will reproduce that mistake.

One offset can be read at several widths. Instance +0x0c is read as a dword (`mtx[0][3] & 8`) in UseInstanceList but as a byte elsewhere, and +0x0d (byte) and +0x0e (ushort) are separate fields. Use the narrowest width plus the neighbouring accesses, not the widest.

Pointer fields in file records only look like dwords until they are resolved in place. CARP::InitResolvers maps each tag to a resolver that runs TagReference::TagReference on specific offsets: Instance +0x1c (InstanceResolver, stride 0x40), BaseDesc +0x0/+0xc/+0x34 (FUN_00118180, which also first writes the tag 'Name' into +0x34), MapNode +0x0 (WorldNodeResolver, 4 x 0x10). Those resolvers are the best evidence for which words are pointers, and the record stride comes from their loops, since file records have no FastAlloc size.

Self-relative and file-relative offsets look like small integers. MapNode +0x8 is a ushort byte offset from the node itself to a ushort index list, and +0xa is an index into that list (only the *2 scale in the asm tells which is which). UGroup data pointers are relative when bit 1 of +4 is set. None of these should be typed as pointers.

Recursion turned into loops fakes linked lists. Xbox WTree::InitializeTree and WalkTree turn the 4th recursive call into a loop, `param_1 = *param_1 + 0x30`, which reads like a next-pointer walk through +0x30. It is actually children[3] of a 4 x 0x10 child array. Compare with PS2 InitializeTree (4 explicit recursive calls).

Names in a class namespace can be misleading. PS2 CARP::BaseDesc::CalcAdjacentZones is a lexicographical_compare over two char ranges (4 pointer args, no this), and PS2 RSceneObj::GetBaseDesc carries a bogus extra param. The RSceneObj pilot's 'baseDesc byte +0x1e==1 -> drawLast' is really Instance->articleDesc (+0x1c) byte +0x1e: UseInstanceList reads *(*(inst+0x1c)+0x1e). BaseDesc::CalcDamageZone's argument is a CARP::Effect, not a BaseDesc. Don't name fields from a namespace method unless its `this` is proven.

Some fields are only touched outside the class. WTargetable +0x41 onScreen is written only by WTargetPicker::UpdateTargets and never initialised by any ctor. +0x28/+0x2c get their meaning only in UpdateTargets. +0x38 is set only by callers after construction (GetWorldTarget, AIVehicle GetTarget, EFireWeapon) and tested by Missile/SetTarget. The picker reaches the objects through std::list nodes (node[2]), so a script has to follow data flow through container nodes and scan every class's code, not just WTargetable::*.

Some offsets are type-tag unions. WTargetable +0x44 is a PhysicsObject*, AICharacter* or AIVehicle* depending on +0x34 (1/2/3), and each branch reads different owner offsets (+0x48/+0x4a, +0x40 and vtable slot 1, +0x10/+0x68). Unioning the accesses would produce a nonsense owner struct. Type it void* and note the discriminator.

Bitfields: Instance +0x3c packs three 10-bit quantised dimensions, a scale-select bit and an isBox bit, all through dword masks. PS2 decompiles GetBoundingRadius as returning `&DAT_00386b80 + (v>>0x1c & 4)`, which is garbage. Derive bit semantics from the setter (CARP::Instance::SetDimensions) and not the decompiled getters.
RTTI isn't evidence of a vtable. PS2 has CARP::Instance_type_info_function ('Q24CARP8Instance') although Instance has no vptr: +0x3c is data on both builds, where GCC would put the vptr last.

Decompiler artifacts on null paths: Xbox GetWorldTarget shows `uRam00000038 = 1` on the FastAlloc-failed branch (the member store at +0x38 applied to a null result). An access scan must not turn that into a global or a separate object.

The same method can treat a field differently on each build. DistFromScreenCenter subtracts resX/2,resY/2 on Xbox but not on PS2 (PS2 screen coords are centred), and camera position is RCamera +0x40 on Xbox vs +0x30 on PS2. So comparing expressions across builds to confirm a field match has to tolerate per-platform constants, and must not treat the camera struct's shift as a shift of the target struct.
notes: WTargetable has no base and no vtable; the targets-in-world list is a std::list<WTargetable*> held by WTargetPicker (+0x2c), and each node's third word points to the object.

Owner types: 0 = fixed point (ctor(x,y,z) 0xcd930: EnableTarget without physics, GetWorldTarget, EFireWeapon), 1 = PhysicsObject (0xcdba0: EnableTarget, EnableTargetBeacon, AIVehicle GetTarget, PBondCar, Simulate), 2 = AICharacter (0xcd9b0: AICharacterEnemyGround/Sunroof ctors), 3 = AIVehicle (0xcda20: AIHelicopter::EnableTargetBeacon).
WTargetPicker::GetSelectedTarget reading Xbox +0x41 against PS2 +0x44 is the bool-packing effect, not a vtable shift. Under the +4 rule it would have been +0x48.

The 'as  ' record that CARP::Instance+0x1c points to deserves its own struct (probably the article/model description): +0 CARP::BaseDesc*, +4 CARP::Effect* (0x40-byte effects, terminated by byte +0x14==0), +8 CARP::AnimInfo* (16-byte entries: +0 keyframe ptr, +8 ushort count, +0xf byte rate), +0xc TagReference, +0x1a/+0x1b system ids (Handle::Create copies them from animInfo +4/+6), +0x1c byte count of 8-byte entries at +0x20 (TagReference at +4), +0x1d draw pass (DrawInstance compares it with the pass to send to the translucent list), +0x1e drawLast. Resolver FUN_00118220.
World tree header at *(WWorld::fgWorld+0x1c): [0] root CARP::MapNode*, [7]/[8]/[9] origin x/y/z, [0xb] root cell size (RSceneObj ctor, UpdatePosition, GenerateCurtainsAndNodes).

RAnimEngine::Handle holds per-instance 64-byte copies of the CARP::Instance records at Handle+0x40*(i+1), so a script scanning accesses to 'Instance' offsets will also see them through Handle (flags byte at entry+0xc, +0xd, +0xe ushort, +0x1c articleDesc).

Every CARP layout was checked on PS2 at the same offsets: SetMapNode/InitializeTree/FindVisibleTreeNodesAndCurtains (MapNode), GetBoundingDimensions/GetCollisionGeometry/CalcDamageZone (BaseDesc), GetPosition/GetBoundingRadius/SetDimensions (Instance).
